name: non-copyable-mixin
intent: Make duplication of an identity-bearing type unrepresentable: the type declares that it has exactly one owner, so the toolchain rejects every copy instead of relying on documentation, removing whole classes of double-free, double-close and duplicated-handle bugs.
problem: A type owns a resource or an identity that cannot be meaningfully duplicated - a file descriptor, connection, lock, transaction, session, credential - yet the language silently supplies copy construction and copy assignment (or an opt-in clone protocol), so sooner or later a copy appears: two owners of one resource that both release it, or two supposedly identical objects whose identities then diverge.
context: Applies to resource-owning and identity-bearing types: RAII handles, sessions, locks, transaction objects, unique owners in concurrent designs, and helper types in generic code where an accidental copy must be a build failure. The mechanism depends on the toolchain - declaration-level refusal in C++, Rust and Swift, reference semantics in the JVM/.NET family, a static-analysis sentinel in Go, hand-written runtime guards in Python and Ruby - so the decision also has to say how ownership may be transferred instead of copied.
benefits: Compile-time refusal where the language supports it: the copy expression is rejected while the code is built, not diagnosed in production, and the diagnostic names the deleted operation or the non-copyable type.
Zero runtime cost: the mechanism is an empty base or a deleted declaration, so the guarantee adds no flag checks, no exceptions and no storage (empty-base optimization applies).

The intent is visible in the declaration itself (private base in the base-specifier list, `= delete` next to the constructor, `~Copyable` on the type), so readers learn the ownership rule without reading documentation.
The copy-suppression rule is written once - a mixin base, a project-wide deleted-member convention, a sentinel type - instead of being repeated (and forgotten) in every class.

Forces the ownership question to be answered early: once copies are gone the author must state how ownership moves (move constructor, consuming parameter, factory hand-off) or that it is shared (reference counting, pointers).
Removes a test class: there is no copy behaviour to test, and typo-prone manual guards (isClosed flags, reference counts) disappear where the compiler does the checking.
tradeoffs: Copy removal is viral: one non-copyable member or base makes every aggregate non-copyable too, so containers and APIs drift toward pointers, references and explicit moves - code that used to be values becomes pointer plumbing.
It destroys value semantics, and transfer must be written explicitly (move constructor/assignment, consuming parameters, ownership hand-off functions), which pushes work onto every caller.
Removing copies while keeping moves is error-prone in C++: declaring the copy operations suppresses the implicit move operations, so a type can silently become non-movable instead of move-only.

On toolchains without declaration-level enforcement (Go, Python, Ruby, JavaScript) the guarantee degrades to a vet check or a runtime guard: a mis-copy fails late - ignored vet output, a TypeError in a production path, or a byte-wise copy of a struct whose definition is visible.
The classic pre-C++11 form (private, undefined copy operations) yields access/link diagnostics rather than a clear compile error, and empty definitions make copies legal for members and friends.

Private inheritance adds an implementation-detail inheritance axis and demands a protected non-virtual destructor, so the type cannot be destroyed polymorphically through the mixin - and the mixin must stay empty to remain free.
Applying it speculatively blocks a later value-like use; removing the guarantee afterwards is an API break for every caller that relied on copying.

participants.responsibility: Declares copy construction and copy assignment unavailable (deleted, private and undefined, or suppressed by a type modifier) and keeps constructor/destructor protected so it can only be used as a base; it stays empty, so it must not add size or runtime cost.
The resource- or identity-bearing class that acquires the guarantee; its declaration (base-specifier list, deleted members, type modifier) is where the ownership rule becomes readable.

The compiler, type checker or analyzer that rejects the generated copy operations at the earliest point available: translation time in C++/Rust/Swift, type checking in TypeScript, `go vet -copylocks` in Go, a raising copy hook where the runtime cannot check.
The operations that remain legal so ownership can still move without duplication: move construction/assignment, consuming parameters, `Option::take`/`mem::replace`, explicit hand-off functions.

The only sanctioned way to create an instance (private constructor, static factory, module-level function), so no second instance is produced by accident where the language cannot refuse construction.

use_cases: RAII and ownership handles: file and socket descriptors, database connections, lock/mutex guards, transaction objects that must be released exactly once.
Identity-bearing domain objects - sessions, credentials, tokens, transfer-like state machines - where a duplicate is a second identity rather than a copy of the state.
Unique owners in concurrent designs: channel endpoints, task handles and single-owner buffers that must not be cloned into two racing owners.
Generic/template helper types (scope guards, generators, lock holders) whose accidental copy must be rejected by the compiler before it is instantiated into a bug.
Aggregates that own a non-shareable member and must not become copyable by accident through an implicitly generated copy constructor.
Rust standard-library resource handles such as `std::fs::File` and `std::net::TcpStream`: moving transfers ownership, while `try_clone` is an explicit opt-in to a second OS handle.
Swift 5.9 `~Copyable` structs and enums for unique resource wrappers: SE-0390 makes copying a compile-time error and pairs the type with borrowing and consuming operations.
Boost.Core's `boost::noncopyable` and modern C++11 `= delete` declarations for RAII classes: the systems prevent accidental copies while leaving the move policy explicit.
avoid_when: The type's copies are meaningful - money, dates, addresses, DTOs, measurements: two equal instances are interchangeable, so keep value semantics (and prefer immutability).
Ownership is genuinely shared: use reference counting or a shared pointer/guard (intrusive-reference-counting) instead of forbidding duplication.
The type must live inside value-based containers, sort/search algorithms or copy-on-write structures; without moves or stable indirection the pattern costs more than it saves.
A single accidental copy path is the real problem: a private factory, a review rule or an immutability convention is cheaper than a guarantee that propagates to every aggregate.
You only need to stop *implicit* copies while explicit ones stay legal - that is a different (weaker) idiom; do not label it non-copyability.
anti_patterns: Copy-suppression as a substitute for ownership design: deleting copies on a type that is really a value (money, dates) and then hand-rolling transfer functions to work around the lost value semantics.
Inheriting publicly from the non-copyable base ('is-a NonCopyable'), leaking an implementation detail into the type's interface and re-opening the question for every subclass.
In C++11 and later, declaring the copy operations private without definitions: experts read it, everybody else gets an access or link error instead of a deleted-function diagnostic.
Empty-bodied private copy operations (pre-C++11): copies stay legal for members and friends, so the class is not actually non-copyable.
Guarding duplication at runtime (throwing from a copy/clone method, flag checks) where the language could have refused at compile time - a failed build is cheaper than a failed production path.
Adding the mixin defensively to every resource type and then aggregating those types by value, so non-copyability propagates and the codebase turns into pointer soup.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: encode the ownership rule in the type system so the toolchain checks it, not the reviewer.
Rule of zero/three/five: state the copy and move policy explicitly instead of inheriting the compiler's defaults.
Single responsibility and RAII: one owner per resource, released deterministically by the owning type.
Explicit over implicit: the refusal belongs to the declaration (base-specifier list, deleted member, type modifier), not to a comment.
Encapsulation: the mechanism is an implementation detail (private inheritance, private factory), never part of the public interface.
Fail fast: reject the misuse at the earliest point - compilation if possible, static analysis next, runtime only as a last resort.
best_practices: Prefer the language's native mechanism (`= delete`, `~Copyable`, reference semantics) and use the base-class mixin only to state the intent recognisably or to standardise it across many types.
Close both copy paths (constructor and assignment), and delete or default all five special members so the move story is explicit.
Keep the mixin an implementation detail: private inheritance or an embedded sentinel, protected non-virtual destructor, no public 'is-a NonCopyable' relationship.
Provide the transfer operation in the same change (move constructor, consuming parameter, hand-off factory); non-copyable and unmovable is almost never what you want.

Where the language cannot enforce it, name the strongest available substitute - `go vet -copylocks`, a raising `__copy__`/`initialize_copy`, a `#`-branded instance - and document the guarantee as best-effort.
Lock the guarantee in with a test: a compile-fail case or `static_assert(!std::is_copy_constructible<T>::value)` in the language's idiom.
Say why at the declaration site ('owns fd; a copy would double-close') so a later cleanup does not remove the mixin.
sources: Wikibooks, More C++ Idioms - 'Non-copyable Mixin' (language-idiom catalogue: private base with suppressed copy operations, plus the documented CRTP variant).
Scott Meyers, Effective C++ (3rd ed., 2005), Item 6: 'Explicitly disallow the use of compiler-generated functions you do not want' - the classic declaration-only form.
